finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the string starts with "https://". That does not restrict the destination host, so an attacker can make the server request internal or cloud-metadata hosts that serve HTTPS, such as https://users.internal, https://localhost, https://127.0.0.1, or an internal host with a TLS listener. A hostname that resolves to a private IP (DNS rebinding) also passes. axios follows redirects by default (maxRedirects 5), and a redirect can reach an http:// internal target, so an attacker-controlled https server can 302 to http://169.254.169.254/ or http://users.internal:8080/. The response body is not returned, but the byte count is, which is a blind oracle: it gives reachability, response size, and error differences for port and host scanning.

trace.note: Only validation: typeof string and startsWith("https://"). No host/IP allowlist, no private-range blocking, no DNS resolution check.
axios.get(url) with default redirect following, so the https-only check is bypassed via redirect
img.data.length returned to the client, giving a blind response-size signal

finding.guards_checked: The https:// prefix check is the only guard and is insufficient. No hostname allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local IP filtering, no DNS pinning, and no maxRedirects:0 or redirect re-validation. There is no authentication middleware. Response size is not capped.

verdict.guard_found: none (only a scheme prefix check: typeof string && startsWith("https://") at server.js:11; no auth middleware, no host allowlist, default axios redirects)
verdict.reason: server.js:10-14 passes the attacker-controlled req.body.avatarUrl to axios.get with only the scheme-prefix check at line 11, with no auth, host allowlist, or redirect restriction, and server.js:15 returns the byte count as a blind oracle.
